items.title: A 95% confidence interval does NOT mean there's a 95% chance the true value is in it
items.claim: Common claim: 'we are 95% confident the mean is between 4.2 and 5.7'. Often interpreted as 'there's a 95% probability the true mean is in this range'. In frequentist statistics this interpretation is technically wrong.
items.prompt: What does a 95% confidence interval actually mean?

options.text: The probability the parameter is in the interval is 95%

If you repeated the experiment many times and constructed a CI each time, 95% of those intervals would contain the true value. For a single interval, the true value is either in it or not — the 95% refers to the procedure's long-run reliability, not to a probability about the parameter
It's the same as a Bayesian credible interval

items.reveal:
In FREQUENTIST statistics, the true parameter (e.g., true mean mu) is treated as fixed, not random. The interval is random because it depends on the random sample. The interval either contains mu or it doesn't — probability 0 or 1.

The '95%' is a property of the PROCEDURE for generating the interval: across many hypothetical replications of the experiment, 95% of the intervals would contain the true mu. For your one observed interval, it either contains mu or doesn't.

In BAYESIAN statistics, the parameter is treated as random (described by a posterior distribution). A 95% credible interval IS the range where the parameter has 95% posterior probability of lying. The Bayesian interpretation is the one most people intuitively want.

Frequentist CIs and Bayesian credible intervals often look similar numerically — but they mean different things. The interpretation matters for inference and communication.

Why this distinction matters:
- Misinterpreting CIs leads to overconfidence in single results.
- Policy debates often hang on whether 'we are 95% sure' means anything actionable.
- Multiple comparisons (running many tests, picking 'significant' ones) inflate apparent CI coverage — see also: replication crisis.

Many statisticians (including Hoekstra et al. 2014) have shown that researchers across disciplines misinterpret CIs.

For most practical purposes, the Bayesian interpretation 'works'. But understanding the frequentist meaning matters for understanding what randomized inference does and doesn't guarantee.
items.why: Statistical results are commonly miscommunicated. Confidence intervals are a famous example: most users (including professionals) believe an interpretation the statistics don't support. Understanding the distinction is part of statistical literacy.

items.title: Doubling something is a 100% increase, NOT a 200% increase
items.claim: Going from 10 to 20: the value has doubled. It has also increased by 100% (an increase of 10 from a base of 10). Headlines often say 'doubled' and '200% increase' interchangeably. They're not the same.
items.prompt: What's the relationship between '__ times' and '__ percent increase'?

options.text: Multiplying by n is the same as a (n - 1) * 100 percent INCREASE; doubling is 100% increase, tripling is 200% increase, quadrupling is 300% increase, etc.
Multiplying by n equals an n*100 percent increase

items.reveal:
Percent increase = (new - old) / old * 100.
Multiplier = new / old.

Doubling: multiplier = 2 = (1 + 1) = original + 100% of original. Therefore a 100% increase.
Tripling: multiplier = 3 = (1 + 2) = 200% increase.
Multiplying by 10: 900% increase.

If prices rise from 50 to 55:
- 'A 10% rise.'
- 'Now 110% of the old price.'
- 'Now 1.1 times the old.'

All equivalent. The common error: 'My income tripled' often presented as '300% growth' instead of '200% growth'.

Why it matters:
- Financial reporting: 'inflation is 200%' could mean prices tripled OR doubled depending on the speaker's confusion.
- Headlines: 'cases up 300%' often means prices QUADRUPLED but is mistaken to mean tripled.
- Scientific papers: 'a 50% reduction' is a multiplier of 0.5; sometimes misread as halving's opposite.

The safe formulation: state the multiplier ('cases multiplied by 4') OR the new value ('cases reached 400%' meaning 4x original). 'Percent increase' is ambiguous in conversation.
items.why: We use percent language fluently but inconsistently. A 100% increase doubles; a 200% increase triples; people routinely confuse the two and report misleading numbers.

items.title: The simplest population equation in the world becomes chaotic
items.claim: Logistic map: x_(n+1) = r * x_n * (1 - x_n). At r = 2.5, x converges to a fixed point. At r = 3.2, it oscillates between two values. At r = 3.7, the values look random. The system is deterministic but unpredictable.

options.text: Nothing — the system is always periodic

Period-doubling cascade: a single fixed point splits into a 2-cycle, then a 4-cycle, then 8, 16, 32... at geometrically closer values of r (Feigenbaum's constant ~4.669). Beyond ~3.5699, the system becomes chaotic
Only mathematicians can see the difference
The chaos is a calculation error

items.reveal_title: Period doubling and the road to chaos
items.reveal:
The logistic map x_(n+1) = r * x_n * (1 - x_n) was introduced by Robert May (1976) as a simple model of population growth with carrying capacity.

For r between 0 and 1: x converges to 0.
For r between 1 and 3: x converges to a non-zero fixed point.
At r = 3: the fixed point becomes unstable; period-2 cycle appears.
At r ≈ 3.449: period-4 cycle appears.
At r ≈ 3.544: period-8.
At r ≈ 3.5644: period-16.

The period-doublings occur at geometrically closer r-values, with ratio approaching Feigenbaum's constant delta ≈ 4.669 — a universal constant of period-doubling bifurcations, appearing in many physical systems (dripping faucet, electronic circuits, fluid dynamics).

At r ≈ 3.5699: 'Edge of chaos'. Beyond this, the system becomes chaotic — small differences in initial conditions grow exponentially.

Within the chaos there are 'islands of stability' (e.g., a period-3 window near r ≈ 3.83). The bifurcation diagram has fractal structure.

This system shows that deterministic dynamics can produce apparent randomness. It motivated chaos theory in the 1970s-80s.

Applications:
- Population biology (when not too realistic).
- Cryptography (pseudo-random number generators).
- Modelling complex systems (transitions to turbulence).
- Analogies to neural and economic dynamics.

The logistic map is a foundational example in the study of dynamical systems and has become a textbook reference for chaos.
items.why: Even the simplest equations can produce unpredictable behaviour. Determinism doesn't guarantee predictability — chaos can emerge from one-line iterations. This insight overturned 19th-century certainty about Newtonian mechanics.
